utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. May I introduce Ms. Kyriaki Karnezi from Greece, who's been with our team since the beginning of September. She has graduated from the University of Groningen with a master's in international criminal law. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Erceg, when we adjourned yesterday we had been looking at paragraphs 22 and 34 of your statement concerning your assertions that the ARK and the ARK institutions were formed due to the impossibility of communications with Pale. And we had looked at the date of establishment of the ARK, but this morning I'd like to turn to the claims you make about the communication problem. Now, in paragraph 22 you state that the ARK was formed because "all communication lines were severed." In paragraph 29 you essentially repeat that assertion saying there was a "total breakdown of telephone lines, all forms of communication." You say that "all the communication lines with us had been severed." Now, with respect to this total breakdown of communication that you allege, you also acknowledge in paragraph 4 that in some mysterious way the instructions on establishing Crisis Staff, that is, the Djeric instructions of approximately April 26 somehow made it through this impenetrable barrier, right, you acknowledge that the Djeric instructions were received?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can remember I had them, but I'm not sure when. I don't know if it was those first few days when it arrived in Banja Luka. I imagine it was within two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And that appears to be the sole "exception" to the receipt of documents from Pale mentioned in your statement, at least mentioned explicitly. Now, in fact, there was another document received from Pale just a couple of days later and that is 1D09858, an enactment of yours reflects the receipt of an order from the Ministry of Defence. Let's take a quick look at that document. Okay, and that's dated the 29th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was sent to Mr. Radic, the president of the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- and it refers to a document received from the republic-level authorities and refers to action that should be taken in response to that; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the reason this document is not acknowledged in your statement as yet another exception to this total breakdown that you claim existed is because it was mentioned, in fact, in one of your drafts but then it was deleted from the final version of your statement that was submitted to this Trial Chamber. In other words, even though you were expressly aware of this document, it was removed from your statement so that this Trial Chamber would not be aware of yet another document that was received from Pale during that period?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot be aware or unaware of this document because I'd never seen it. It was not sent to me personally or to the institution that I was in. It was sent to the president of the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka, not the president of the Executive Council of the AR Krajina. That's why I'm not aware of this document. I don't remember anything, any of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we have 1D09853, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But do we know who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, if we wait for just a moment, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- I think we'll at least have part of that answer and then we can pursue it further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it was sent to the president of Municipal Assembly, but was -- by who was it sent?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Erceg, I believe that's a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was sent by the Executive Council, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you see the heading of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Exactly, Excellency. Thank you. It doesn't originate from Sarajevo at all --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no. If you could read the heading, it says: "Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. "Autonomous Region of Krajina. "Executive Council. "Banja Luka." We can collapse the English for the moment for the benefit of the -- and can you show him the signature part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Yes, yes, that's correct, now I see that it passed through the institution of the Executive Council of the AR Krajina. It was probably just transmission there, sending this document to the municipalities. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not. Just a moment, please. It is typewritten. It says "Nikola Erceg," but it's somebody else's signature. Probably I didn't even know about this document, somebody else forwarded it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And we were -- we have been in the process of calling up 1D09853. And if we could turn to portion where we'd find paragraph 37. Okay. This document is one of the previous drafts prepared by you and the Karadzic team, and it says: "I have been shown document 1D9858," that's the document we just looked at. "This enactment of mine relies on an order of the Ministry of Defence which was one of the rare enactments of that kind to arrive in the ARK from Pale, but I do not remember how ..." So you looked at this document before, you acknowledged that it reflected the receipt of --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the answer is yes?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, now I see that it is being confirmed that I had the document, but I didn't know at that moment, it's just when I read this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. So whose idea was it to take this paragraph out of your statement, a statement which alleged that there was a total breakdown in communications, notwithstanding the fact that this document got through?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no way of knowing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Let's take a look at another of the documents that somehow appeared in the ARK despite your claims of this impenetrable barrier. And I'd like to look first at P2824, English and B/C/S pages 4. This is an extract from the telegram log-book of the republic communications centre, and if we look at the bottom of the page in both languages we see a reference to a telegram from the republic-level authorities to the autonomous districts, including Banja Luka, which refers to the dissociation from the participation of Pejanovic and Kecmanovic in the BH Presidency. And the date is -- of this telegram is June 5th, 1992. Now, just to orient the Trial Chamber, Pejanovic and Kecmanovic were the two Serb representatives who had garnered the most votes in the 1990 elections behind Plavsic and Koljevic, and then assumed the positions of Plavsic and Koljevic when they left the Bosnian Presidency; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the dissociation being referred to here was a kind of symbolic dissociation; right? It wasn't -- it wasn't any concrete -- it wouldn't have any concrete effect on Pejanovic or Kecmanovic. It was just the political or propaganda position to be taken by the Bosnian Serb authorities in relation to the service of Pejanovic and Kecmanovic on the Bosnian Presidency?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen this document, but the reasoning was as you had set it forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could look next at 65 ter 01558.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a public announcement dated the 6th of June signed by Vojo Kupresanin, the president of the ARK Assembly, expressing on behalf of the Serbian people of Krajina the renunciation of Kecmanovic and Pejanovic. It refers to them as traitors and degenerates, and in conformity with the telegram sent the previous day dissociates itself from any decision these two might sign. So, Mr. Erceg, this public announcement by Kupresanin is clearly a response to the instructions sent from the republic level just the previous day in respect of this propaganda effort; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be put that way in terms of the time when this happened, but Nenad Kecmanovic and Mirko Pejanovic cannot be equated in any way, but it is certain that that's the way it was in the public domain at the time. By the way, may I say that this is the first time I see this press release. I hadn't seen it before in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about the witness -- 1D9858?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, absolutely. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6531, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And this one as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 01558 will be Exhibit P6532.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Erceg, apart from the documents we've just looked at and others, you were aware that there was a military communications system; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as you explained in your interview in 2001, you believed that guide-lines from Pale were forwarded using the military communications system and also the messenger service; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In paragraph 26 you state that you think that relations between Brdjanin and the SDS leadership were good for a time, but then -- but relations change and so much so that at one point Brdjanin left the SDS, et cetera. Just to clarify that, what you said back in July 2001 was that the relationship between Brdjanin and the SDS leadership must have been good not for a time but at the time; that is, at the time that was being discussed in the interview which is basically the time of the outbreak of the war?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know there were oscillations, I mean in respecting certain things, if I can put it this way. The institution of the president of the republic included, so that goes for Brdjanin and for the rest. So there were oscillations, yes, vis-a-vis everyone, not only Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, no, I appreciate that as a general matter, but that's a -- that's a bit vague and tends to obscure the actual fact. Brdjanin's problems with leaving the SDS didn't occur until years later; right? That's when he left the SDS, not in May of 1992, first of all.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about these dates. I hear these dates from you and I have no idea what these dates mean. For me what matters is the very essence. All of us had our views regarding the president, including Mr. Brdjanin, and then he formed his party. I don't know why. I don't know whether it was because he quarrelled with President Karadzic. But I know there were tensions, tense situations, between practically all the MPs and the president. That is logical and only natural.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 16, this is a misinterpretation. The witness said there was argumentation, discussion, quarrels, something -- or struggle of views, maybe that would be the right word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Struggle of views.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not views, as was interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we have 1D09896, please, page 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. If we look at the top third of the page, you were asked about the sort of relationship that Mr. Brdjanin had with the republic level. You said, and here the interpreter speaks in the third person in interpreting your answer: "Each of us has ... had a different approach to things, of course, but he cannot say what was the relationship between Brdjanin and the republic SDS, but it must have been good at the time ..." Then you go on to describe that at some point he formed his own party. Toward the bottom of the page the question is asked again: "Sorry, maybe my question was not clear, but a moment ago you said Brdjanin had a good relationship with politicians at the republic level? "A. Yes, there's no question about that. He did have good relations. "Q. With whom, in particular? "A. It's a personal question. How can he say now," referring to you in your answer, "his co-operation with SDS president, with the Assembly members, it was a very good relationship. How close they were, he cannot tell you anything about that, but it was obvious he could feel it, that there was the common goal that they all shared which brought them all together."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then you confirm --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we can scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then if we turn the page, we can see the reference to the common goal they all shared which brought them all together, and then the confirmation by you that when you referred to the SDS president, you were referring to Mr. Karadzic. Now, that's what you said in 2001 about Mr. Brdjanin's relationship with the SDS leadership, and in particular Mr. Karadzic, that it was good at the time, a very good relationship, it was obvious, and you could feel that the common goal they all shared brought them together; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in approximately page 11 of your statement, you deal with a number of matters under the heading of powers of the ARK with respect to the republican organs. And that means the powers of the Autonomous Region of Krajina with respect to the Republika Srpska republic organs; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in paragraph 58 you refer to an extract from the 15th ARK Assembly Session held on the 4th of March, 1992, reflecting a decision to form ARK public funds, that's a reference to D04094. And in the same paragraph you refer to the fact that: "We leaders of the ARK took it upon ourselves to do that and under normal circumstances these areas would have been regulated at the level of the republic." Similarly, in paragraph 59, you cite a report from the session of the ARK Assembly on the same day, which you say confirms the decision to establish a CSB for the region of Bosanska Krajina from part of the republican MUP, and thus transfer the authority of the republican MUP to the CSB, the Security Services Centre, in Banja Luka. Now, Mr. Erceg, these events occurred at a time when the joint government still existed, when there was -- when there was still a Bosnian government in which the full coalition served, that is, SDA representatives, HDZ representatives, SDS representatives; right? The conflict had not yet occurred and the government was still in existence?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The government did exist, but that was not our government.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But the impact of decentralising the funds from the SDK and having them controlled by the Krajina and the impact of removing authority from the republican MUP was on the Bosnian government, on the joint government that existed at that time. It was removal of authority from them; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The setting up of the funds and financial institution and the setting up of the SDK is the result of the fact that we didn't have communication with our central government at Pale. This is not about the government in Sarajevo. Everything I'm saying in this sense is due to the fact that there was no communication between the AR Krajina and the government at Pale, the government of the Serbian people, that is. Why are you talking about the government in Sarajevo? It was war time, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Are you asserting that the war had broken out by the beginning of March, 1994 [sic], and that there was an RS government in -- and political structure established in Pale at the beginning of March 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to war, I believe that the war started when Izetbegovic said that there should be sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but now you have to talk about nuances. What is the war? The fact that the state can no longer exist or that there is a front line? It's a very relative thing. The beginning of a war is a very relative thing. How things developed is one matter, but we had to cope with all those situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Erceg, nothing relative about it, and I'm not talking -- I'm not asking you for an ideological dissertation. I asked you whether the joint government still existed at the beginning of March 1992, something I thought you confirmed before. You referred to the government, the RS government in Pale. So I asked you whether you were stating to this Court that you, that is, your testimony, that Mr. Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb authorities had moved to Pale and set up their structures by the beginning of March 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you when that was, whether that was in March or April, I'm not sure, but it did happen. The most important thing here is that it did happen. It doesn't really matter when that happened. It's of a lesser importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Erceg, it matters in terms of the purpose and effect of the actions which you pointed out in your statement because if the joint government still existed then they had the effect of destabilising and undermining the joint government. So let me put to you this proposition that we've addressed in this Court before and this Court has received evidence on. The purpose of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and other autonomous -- and other regions was to resist the movement by Muslims and Croats toward a sovereign and independent Bosnia and, in effect, to destroy the joint government, to destroy the Bosnian government. And that's what -- correct or not? You knew that.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not correct. It was not to destroy the Bosnian government. It was for us to survive, so this was not about the destruction of the government. Why? However, so much time later, of course I have forgotten a lot of things. What I said ten years ago was obviously more accurate than what I'm saying now. Obviously what I said in those interviews would be more accurate because in the meantime I have forgotten a lot of things. I can't say how sure I am about some of the details that I myself shared with the investigators because of course time is important and time matters, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Among other things, this Court has received the following evidence: That at the 20th Assembly Session in August or September 1992, Mr. Kupresanin said: "Last year we built up the region and made it strong with a clear purpose and goal. The task of the region of Krajina was to destroy Alija's state." That's D456, page 70 in the English, page 76 in the B/C/S. Mr. Mijatovic said at the same session at page 68 in the English, page 75 of the B/C/S: "At a time when we had to destroy a unitary Bosnia, the SAO regions and districts were politically and territorially the best solution." And at the 36th Assembly Session, P1083, at English page 11, B/C/S 13, Mr. Krajisnik confirmed that: "The establishment of the autonomous districts was a response to the centralisation of power in the hands of the Muslim/Croat coalition." And further explained that once they fulfilled their functions, they were abolished by amendments to the constitution. So does this refresh your memory in any way that the purpose of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and the other regions and districts was, in effect, to destroy the Bosnian state and prevent the possibility of a sovereign and independent Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, can we -- objection. Why my learned friend Mr. Tieger does not repeat the following wording: Alija's state, not the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We are not supposed to redefine the gist of the matter through one's questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. I think Mr. Tieger read out the quotes and he put his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Erceg, you were about to answer the question. Can you do that or do you need to have me repeat the last line --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, well, I mean I take it I don't have to repeat everything I just read to you; if I do, I will. But I asked you if this refreshes your memory in any way that the purpose of the ARK, the Autonomous Region of Krajina, and the other regions and districts was, in effect, to destroy the Bosnian state and prevent the possibility of a sovereign and independent Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there was such reasoning. I did not hear Kupresanin say that, but I was present when Mr. Krajisnik said what he did. Of course I cannot claim that he used those exact words, but I can affirm that those things were discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I seem to be getting some odd --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is your mike --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, I think the interpreters had some additional mike on. I just wanted to -- okay, that seems to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Erceg, at paragraph 85 you assert that notwithstanding the general nature of the hierarchy to which you refer in other part of your statement, that Sanski Most acted "completely autonomously," you say a completely autonomous decision with reference to a 4 June 1992 order from the Sanski Most Crisis Staff to the Territorial Defence staff on disarming paramilitary formations in Sanski Most. And you say it's completely autonomous because the Sanski Most Crisis Staff held its own meeting and adopted its own decision and issued an order to its own municipal TO. So setting aside the question of autonomy within that limited realm, the reality, Mr. Erceg, is that this decision actually reflected the hierarchy, beginning with republican level and going down to the municipalities via the intermediate level of the ARK, and in particular with respect to this issue of disarming - isn't that right? - that there was a republican level decision on taking all necessary measures that the ARK acted in response to that in issuing its order to disarm paramilitary formations and then Sanski Most implemented that order in its municipality?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Similarly in paragraph 82, you cite 1D9822, which is conclusions from Prijedor showing -- which you assert show the high degree of independence from the ARK. And in that connection I wanted just to look quickly at whether Prijedor implemented ARK decisions after that time. So if we could look quickly at P2740. That's a 22 June 1992 ARK Crisis Staff decision or it -- that reflects both the decision of the ARK Crisis Staff, prohibiting non-Serbs from many kinds of employment which -- and we see that on page 1 and 2, the ARK decision signed by Mr. Brdjanin. And then at page 3 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S we're able to see the president of the Prijedor Crisis Staff, Mr. Stakic, forwarding the ARK Crisis Staff order for implementation. And then if we could look at P2637, which is dated the 1st of July, a little over a week later. And also the -- I will note -- I don't think we have to return to the previous document, but the ARK Crisis Staff order was numbered 03-53/92. All right. Page 1 refers to the Crisis Staff document we saw a moment ago which was dated the 23rd of June, 1992, that was the page we saw before. And if we turn to the last entry on page 2 of both languages, we can see a reflection of the confirmation that the ARK Crisis Staff order which was forwarded by Dr. Stakic for implementation was, in fact, implemented. Now, clearly, Mr. Erceg, that implementation comes after the date of the document that you cite showing Prijedor's alleged independence. This is a reflection of the fact that Prijedor continued to implement ARK Crisis Staff orders; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on the case. Some decisions from AR Krajina towards the Crisis Staff were implemented. Some couldn't be implemented and for others there was no will to implement them. I don't know what happened. I know that there was disobedience among the municipalities and among the Crisis Staffs in respect of the Crisis Staff of AR Krajina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On lines 3 and 4 there is an error. The witness said that those were the decisions of the Crisis Staff and not the Executive Council of the AR Krajina, and as we read in the transcript one would conclude that it's the other way around. The witness said: These are not things that were issued by the Executive Council of Krajina but by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question was not about Executive Council at all. Do you confirm having said so, Mr. Erceg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure what I'm supposed to say. What do you mean? Do you want me to confirm that I didn't say -- if you're asking me to confirm what I have just said, what I said a couple of minutes ago, then, yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What you said is: Some decisions were implemented and some were not. That was your answer in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I would like to once again make a point that I've made before about the nature of Mr. Tieger's questions to the witness. The last question was so complicated with multiple documents, and then asked the last -- the question was: Right? So right to what? He made a number of assertions in that question. So this is not a good way to get accurate information, and I've suggested before that when he has one document is to just ask: Is this an example of ...? And then put the proposition, then get a clear answer. In this case he got the answer that it depends on the case. So by putting multiple propositions in a single question, we're not advancing the trial at all in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I've actually met with Mr. Robinson on this and I've been reasonably receptive to suggestions where I thought they were well-founded. In this case I don't think it's appropriate. That sequence of events could not usefully have been broken down if it came to one point, and the question was -- I asked exactly what he suggested I should have asked which is very concrete: Was this a reflection of the implementation after the date of the document that he pointed to as a reflection of non-implementation. So it couldn't have been simpler and the witness was able to answer it easily. And I think now Mr. Robinson is introducing a problem where none exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see a point of putting to the witness less documents at one time. Think about that. If you put several questions, it may be complicating the witness in answering the question. We'll be better off with less documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that, if I may, so I won't belabour this, but I discussed that with Mr. Robinson, I understood his point in that respect -- in that regard, and I am more than happy to follow that as scrupulously as possible. In this case it seemed to me that the sequence was not difficult to follow, that the documents were related, and the proof of that is the fact that I think the witness was easily able to follow it. But I do have it in mind as a general proposition. I think here it was unfair -- that was an unfair comment. But at this point I think we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Erceg, you cannot point me to a single document or single instance where the Prijedor Crisis Staff, or any other Crisis Staff for that matter, refused to follow or implement ARK Crisis Staff decisions about, for example, dismissals, can you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this moment, obviously not. I don't have such documents. Whether there were any, yes, I suppose that there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you are well aware of the fact that the ARK policy on dismissals was, in fact, implemented in the municipalities and many, many non-Serbs were dismissed. And in fact, by the end of 1992 virtually all non-Serbs had been terminated from employment. You know that; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not about the ARK but about the Crisis Staff of the ARK. Please be precise. There were dismissals, yes, but it is not true that everybody was dismissed. It is also true that Serbs were dismissed as well. We insisted on the reciprocity and that is also correct. It was a dynamic situation which cannot be described in just one word. You have to have some very exact data. I don't know whether there are such data available. There were indeed dismissals and those dismissals included Serbs in every municipality, and I repeat that we insisted on reciprocity; i.e., if we heard that somebody was dismissed in a municipality in Bosnia and Herzegovina, obviously there were reactions to that. It is only human, I suppose. But there were no decisions that were -- that said that those things should be done. Obviously there were some wrong-doings in the process, but that was true of both sides across the territory of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is what you have to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At paragraph 91, Mr. Erceg, you state that you were present at meetings of the ARK Crisis Staff when the existence of Omarska and Keraterm was mentioned. And you indicate that these were raised by municipality officials at these meetings who wanted to discuss how to "logistically provide" and how to "finance the whole project." Now, we've heard testimony from -- we've heard that Mr. Kupresanin, for example, stated in 2001 that he knew about events within 15 to 20 days after they happened and knew about Omarska within 15 days of its formation. So how -- how quickly after the establishment of Omarska and Keraterm do you say that these discussions about how to finance the whole project took place in the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say when that was. I'm not aware of the dates. I don't know under what circumstances they were set up; however, when a crisis occurred - and I'm referring to a logistics crisis - I suppose that it was then that the matter was sent for our consideration. I really don't have a clue about the dates when that happened and how much time lapsed between the day when they were founded and our intervention. I really can't say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And you refer to discussions, so there was clearly more than one. How many such discussions were held about Omarska and Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those discussions were part of broader considerations concerning the incarceration of Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in Croatia, and in our midst. Of course those were discussions. It was said that it happened, that the process is underway, and that that process should be fought in every possible way to prevent those things from happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So do I understand you correctly that the discussion of Omarska and Keraterm where non-Serbs were held was part of the discussion about how to deter or respond to the detention of Serbs elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't say that that was the point of our discussions. That happened which opened the door to a process that was very hard to control, and that's why I assume that the reasoning was that if those things were difficult to control or stop, at least we should ease the situation and we should try and minimise the impact of that situation and minimise the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And part of the discussion was that in -- that the number of prisoners -- in other words, there were so many prisoners that it was straining the resources of the municipalities to deal with the -- what you called the whole project. That was part of the discussion; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that the magnitude of that situation was the main preoccupation, that it was the main topic of discussions, no way. However, resources had to be provided, there's no doubt about that. It was at the time when goods were -- became more and more scarce and we had to be rational. And when it came to being rational with food and other bare necessities, we also had to take into account the resources that were necessary to provide food for prisoners, of course. Food was becoming scarce and we had to be careful about all of the provisions, including the food. We had to make sure it was sent where it was needed and when it was needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm just about out of time, Mr. Erceg, so I'm going to deal with one more subject and that appears at paragraph 95 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I don't know exactly my time, but I can just deal with that one subject. I think I'm nearly at the end, but I don't think I'm over yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At paragraph 95 you discuss the issue of expulsions, insisting there was no policy to expel or persecute non-Serbs. Now, in your -- in 2002 during your interview you were asked about the testimony in the Brdjanin case of a man named Amir Dzonlic, who testified that he came to you seeking help for non-Serbs who had been crammed into seven cars -- railroad cars meant for livestock and who were dying of thirst in the summer heat. He said that he came to you for assistance but that you said those people were in transit and that you were not competent to help. And you stated in your interview that you didn't recall that discussion but that if someone had -- felt that if someone had come to you with such a request, you would have felt bound to help. You recall that -- or do you recall that part of your interview, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Amir Dzonlic, as far as I remember, is a man who lived in my own entrance-way and it's not true that he ever addressed me. I know that I saved some people after I met them literally in passing and I would have accommodated him too, if he had ever addressed me, but he didn't and I don't know what he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in 2002, sir, I think you said you didn't recall that. But we'll leave it for the moment. Because you -- it is fair to say, however, that you were aware that non-Serbs were leaving the ARK in great numbers, weren't you? You were aware of that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only confirm what I said before. I don't recall Amir because he didn't address me. How can I remember something that didn't happen? That is a very important thing and it would have remained etched in my memory, but he didn't address me. We never had any contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But my last question was: You were aware, were you not, that non-Serbs were leaving the area, the Autonomous Region of Krajina, in great numbers, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course people were leaving. As far as I know, there was no coercion involved. It was their own desire to leave, but you have to understand, talking about Banja Luka, for instance, these people were in transit so you could have gained the impression that Banja Luka is expelling people which wasn't true. In a large percentage, people were leaving of their own free will.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No coercion? So were you completely oblivious, unaware, of the repeated statements of Mr. Brdjanin in one form or another that Muslims had to go?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, of course in war anything can happen. There was some coercion in some cases but there was no official policy of coercion. Nobody ever said: We have to expel people. But individual cases happened even without a war, let alone in war time. Of course, I'm not saying that these things never happened. Individual cases did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure that's a truism that no one would dispute that there were individual cases. The question is: How many individual cases and for what reason. I asked you and you didn't answer. Were you completely unaware of the repeated statements of the president of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, public statements, some in very ugly forms, that Muslims had to go?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: What can I do about that? He did make those statements. That's done and over with. I personally was against it. But, again I have to say there were forced expulsions but not in the measure people talk about. I think it was Brdjanin's personal interest because he couldn't do it through the Crisis Staff because no official decision had been made to that effect, that he personally was involved in these things is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you aware of the devastation of Muslim villages by the VRS and Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Not at all?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I have to know that? If I had heard anything about it, I could have believed the story or not. From my personal experience, I saw only Kozarac, every house destroyed. And after a while, as the war went on, one couldn't come even near the front line, so you couldn't know what was going on. And by nature, I'm a pacifist and I didn't want to see these things. If I had the opportunity, I would have avoided it. When I travelled to Prijedor, I saw that village - what's the name? The one I mentioned now? - Kozarac. But I know from stories that things were devastated, one, another, then another. I know it only from stories. I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you knew that the VRS was implementing the strategic objectives in the area of the Autonomous Region of Krajina; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the strategic objectives of the army were, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, can we look at 1D9896, e-court pages 70 -- e-court page 78.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There we see a discussing about the strategic objectives: "When did you first hear the reference to them?" We see at the beginning of the page. Well, that's in the previous page. If we can turn to the previous page just to see the beginning of that discussion. At the top of the page we see: "When did you first hear reference to these strategic goals? "At about that time that was during the preparation of the Assembly. "Do you recall who actually spoke about them? "President of the republic, the assembly president, some of the deputies who actually made the speech. "Were they referring" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure the witness can read English, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll be more -- I'll recite that more slowly and carefully. And let me turn to the next page then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were asked: "Did you hear a lot of discussion about these goals among the members of the SDS after the 12th May meeting?" You said: "Discussing it, it's beside the point. This was a strategic goal that was determined and adopted at the session and now we had to -- we were about to implement. But it's totally irrelevant whether discussions about the strategic goals. There's no doubt, yes, of course, we talked about it, but it was." And then you go on to say: "It was a task, it was the army who was sort of, more required to fulfil these tasks, because the civilian structures, the political structures failed in their attempts to stay within one joint, within one state of Yugoslavia. And there was only one alternative to having military structures trying to achieve what the Serbian people wanted. What can civilian, what could civilian authorities do when you have to do was to join two territories that were physically separated. This could have been achieved only through a military operation because at that time we have already had war." That's what you explained in 2001; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have, I think, exhausted my time and that concludes my examination. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I turn to Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Robinson, with respect to the associated exhibit you raised at the end of last -- yesterday's session, the Chamber has reviewed the English translation and is satisfied with its relevance and the nature of -- indispensable and inseparable part of the statement, so it will be admitted. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, before he does that, first maybe is the exhibit number to be given now?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D4109, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: And before Dr. Karadzic begins his re-examination, I just wanted to put something on the record, and that is that on the 14th of November of this year you told us that we should only tender associated exhibits which form an indispensable part of the statement and that we -- which are significant to our case, and you asked us to be more vigilant and take more robust care in tendering exhibits. And when you did that, I took it upon myself to tell my team that I would examine every statement and make sure that the exhibits that are included in those statements are, in fact, meeting your criteria. And the first statement that I took up was Mr. Erceg's, and I eliminated nine documents from that statement which I believed were not necessarily significant to the case or indispensable to the statement. And one of those documents was 1D9858, which was the subject of Mr. Tieger's question to the witness. So I just wanted to put that on the record in case Mr. Tieger wanted to ask any further questions of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Erceg.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us be mindful of the breaks between question and answer, as always when we speak the same language. On page 25 today you were asked if you had heard about any Muslim or Croat villages, or rather, some villages, I believe Muslim and Croat ones were meant, that were devastated. Did you hear about any Muslim or Croat villages that remained intact?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any information about what it depended on?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: On our position on the war and our desire to avoid war at all costs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 24 you were asked about Brdjanin and how he said that Muslims and Croats had to leave. Did you ever hear him personally speak like that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Occasionally in informal conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 13 of today's LiveNote a quotation was made of Mr. Kupresanin, saying that Alija's state had to be destroyed. What did we understand by this term, "Alija's state"?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very broad concept. Alija's state was a centralised state within the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Its objective was to dominate over everyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the ideological basis of what we call Alija's state?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ideological underlying concept of that state was undoubtedly the Islamic Declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long do the demands of Krajina and other regions for the decentralisation of funding date back, that is, the demand that funding not be centralised, that it flow back to regions?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the former Bosnia-Herzegovina or the government of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How long had such demands been heard in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these demands were always heard. I personally am in favour of decentralisation. It's a normal process which is always on the table. It's an issue which is always on the table in every country, but in socialism it couldn't be discussed much. With the introduction of the democratic system, of course some thinking went along those lines but of course within an appropriate framework.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So if there had been no war, would you have gone on insisting on the decentralisation of funding?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally would have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 10 of today's LiveNote, it was read back to you and you confirmed that there was a common goal that held all those aforementioned people together. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what that common goal was?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Living in the rump Yugoslavia as a socio-political system; the other goal was to avoid war wherever possible; the third goal was to continue living as our own lords and masters on our own land.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see P6531. It was admitted a moment ago. Could we zoom in on the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm a little confused. There's nothing in the middle of the stamp, it doesn't even say "Republika Srpska," just the Republic of Bosnia or perhaps the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Autonomous Region of Krajina. Are you familiar with this stamp? Could it have existed at that time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I'm not familiar with this. I don't recognise it. But I see my typewritten signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom out now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm also confused by this passage which says: "Please find attached the order of the commander of the National Defence ..." Did the Territorial Defence have a commander?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We also see a reference number 03, that number appears very often on various documents. What does that number mean?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the protocol, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see now P6532. Can we make this larger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We see the number again, 03.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then it must be the Assembly. It's a document of the Assembly of the ARK.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because you see the connection 03 and Vojo Kupresanin signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But here we see the Executive Council and again 03.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom in on the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How come there is no coat of arms and there is no Serbian Republic of BH?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is everything clear to you about these stamps?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there should be something in the middle, an emblem, something. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday on transcript page 88, document 05415 was shown. It was signed by Mr. Dukic. Can you remember which position he occupied?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I know he was in Sarajevo, but I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To the best of your knowledge did Crisis Staffs exist within the party?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I tell you Mr. Dukic was president of the Executive Board of the party, would he have been in a position to send dispatches like the one we've seen to state authorities?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay, that's a leading question, it's speculative, and it's basically a useless exchange. But -- so I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Erceg, can you explain to the best of your knowledge the difference between the Muslims and Croats who remained in our towns and cities throughout Krajina all the time on the one hand and those who left, who didn't dare to stay?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which difference you mean, you mean loyal versus disloyal?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, why were some able to stay and others weren't?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some of course were able to say if they wanted to go on living there peacefully within the limits of the situation, and those who wanted more than was their due. And of course there were those who wanted something different; that is to say a Muslim who wanted to join the Muslim army and a Croat who wanted to join the Croatian army. At certain times there were even large waves of these departures, convoys were organised, but again, only if they wished to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And speaking of pressure, who exerted pressure, those who wanted to leave or the authorities on them?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The authorities did not exert any pressure. In a very large percentage of cases, it was their own wish to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And my last question: Did you know what my position was regarding forcible transfers?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: You never insisted on that. You never said any such thing publicly. I suppose you wanted first to avoid war and once war started you wanted it waged in a dignified way, if I can put it that way, without perpetrating any evil. That's how I experienced it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Erceg. Thank you for making the effort to come here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Erceg. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the Chamber go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00 in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Shall we rise for some five or ten minutes? Five minutes. We'll rise for five minutes. --- Break taken at 11.24 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sajic. Please make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Sajic. Could you please tell us your rank which I would like to use in our further communication.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. My name is Milorad Sajic. I am a teacher of defence and reserve lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Lieutenant-Colonel, we have to speak slowly and we have to pause between my questions and your answers. Did you provide my Defence team a statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did provide a statement to your Defence team and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D9531 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that statement on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read the statement and did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I read it and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the last page to identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement accurately reflect what you said to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it accurately reflects my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today in the courtroom, the same ones you were asked by my Defence team members, would your answers be the same in essence?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this statement into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is the Defence also tendering associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We had listed three associated exhibits; however, one has since been admitted, that's 0941 now admitted as -- excuse me, 09421 now admitted as D4051. And we're tendering the other two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any objection, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They will be all admitted into evidence. Shall we assign the numbers for them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The 92 ter statement 1D9531 will be Exhibit D4114. 65 ter number 1D9850 will be Exhibit D4115. And 1D9851 will be Exhibit D4116.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm now going to read a short summary of Lieutenant-Colonel's statement in English. [In English] In 1991 Milorad Sajic was appointed commander of the Territorial Defence in the Banja Luka municipality, and during the spring and summer of 1992 Mr. Milorad Sajic was a secretary of the regional secretariat of national defence, for which position he was not either nominated or recommended by the Serbian Democratic Party. He has never been a member of the same. Mr. Sajic became a member of the ARK Crisis Staff in 1992 and the member of the Army of Republika Srpska. In 1992, after -- in 2000, I suppose -- so after the war he was demobilised. In March 1992, Milorad Sajic took the position of a commander of Banja Luka Territorial Defence, appointed at this position by the Municipal Assembly on a proposal of the president of the Municipal Assembly and based on the opinion issued by the commander of the republican Territorial Defence. The direct superior of Milorad Sajic at this -- at the time was the commander of the district Territorial Defence staff in Banja Luka, and his superior on the other district -- on the other hand was a commander of the republican Territorial Defence staff of Bosnia and Herzegovina, General Drago Vukosavljevic. Milorad Sajic was also a member of the National Defence Council of municipality of Banja Luka. As a secretary of the Autonomous Region of Krajina National Defence, Milorad Sajic was carrying out the orders of the Ministry of Defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. At the time Nikola Erceg, the president of the Executive Council of the Krajina region, was his superior as well as Minister of Defence, General Subotic. The Yugoslav People's Army reserve forces were recruited from the Autonomous Region of Krajina in 1991 and they were involved in the combat operations in Croatia. As a result of the situation created by the outbreak of the war, high number of Serbian refugees started fleeing to Krajina and the region experienced lack of capacity to solve the thus-created problem. Weapon distribution was enacted in 1991 and 1992 after mobilisation took place. In early April 1992 there was a blockade of Banja Luka by the Serbian Defence Forces, SOS. The issue was discussed on a meeting convened with the presence of Radic, Zupljanin, and Tutus, aiming at the peaceful resolution. There was no existence of a strategic goal to expel Muslims and Croats from the territory of Republika Srpska. On 12th of May, 1992, the Army of Republika Srpska underwent a reorganisation and the Territorial Defence became a part of it. The same process was observed in June 1992 when no special Serbian Territorial Defence was formed, but instead the Territorial Defence units were reorganised into infantry brigades. Following the outbreak of the war, there was a lack of means of communication experienced between the Autonomous Region of Krajina and Pale, and the situation remained the same up until June 1992 when a corridor was forced and communications between Pale and Banja Luka were restored. The war situation necessitated the formation of a Crisis Staff which was headed by Mr. Radic. Milorad Sajic never held the office of vice-president of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Mr. Sajic was present on several meetings of the Crisis Staff chaired by Brdjanin. No penalties used to be imposed in case of non-attendance of the -- there was no actual voting mechanism as regards to the decision-making process within the Crisis Staff. For certain period of time there were regular meetings and reports were prepared accordingly which were supposed to be forwarded to Radovan Karadzic. Although Milorad Sajic was not aware of the set-up or location of camps or collection centres, on one of the meetings of the Crisis Staff representatives from Prijedor had raised the issue concerning shortage of food and clothing supplies. Milorad Sajic claims that the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina was not in capacity to issue orders to General Talic or to Mr. Zupljanin and was not in control of the Banja Luka district Territorial Defence staff. The region of Banja Luka had formed its own Crisis Staff, which was later renamed the War Staff. Milorad Sajic never met Radovan Karadzic in person. A delegation to Pale was planned in May 1992 including himself, Kupresanin, Erceg, and Zupljanin, which was however not realised. And that is a short summary and at that moment I do not have questions for Mr. Sajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sajic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is, through your written witness statement in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Sajic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sajic, at paragraph 12 of your statement you assert that between the outbreak of war and the time -- and late June when the corridor was created there were "no links to Pale." Nevertheless, you acknowledge that you received General Subotic's mobilisation order of the 16th of April, 1992, which is in evidence in this case as P2412. Now, Mr. Sajic, the fact that you received this order from General Subotic implies that your claim that there were no links to Pale at this time is not true. There had to be links in order for you to receive this mobilisation order from General Subotic; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: The mobilisation order from General Subotic, I believe that I received it after the corridor was broken on the 16th of June and my order was on the 4th of May. It could have arrived from the communication centres of municipalities. I really can't remember how I received it. I did not communicate with Subotic at all. I could not get in touch with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sajic, you just said that you received General Subotic's order after the corridor was broken and then you say: "And my order was on the 4th of May ..." Your order of the 4th of May, which is in evidence as P2818, and which you refer to in your statement, states: "Pursuant to decision of the Ministry of National Defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, number 192 of 16 April 1992 ..." And goes on from there. So it is crystal clear that by the 4th of May, 1992, when you implemented General Subotic's order, you had received it; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: No, not fully. I could have received the order a day or two before I issued my own order. If I had received it on the 17 or 18 April, I would have issued mine immediately thereafter. So the links that existed before the corridor was broken through was not really functioning in my view because that order required from me to urgently issue my own order and convey the message of the previous order to all the municipalities. However, I only received that order 20 days later.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sajic, the Chamber's received evidence from the person who actually transmitted General Subotic's order to Banja Luka, and he explained that it was sent by teleprinter, using the teleprinter connection between Pale and Banja Luka. And that's Mr. Vukovic's evidence at P2794, pages 20 to 21. Were you aware that there was a teleprinter connection operating between Pale and Banja Luka at this time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: That was the only connection that I deemed usable, the teleprinter in the centre for information and communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we have P2821, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sajic, this is an 18 June 1992 document from the Ministry of Defence in Pale sent to the other ministries and it says that: "The communications centre at Pale can send telegrams to the Serbian Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina and to other Serbian autonomous regions ..." Now, you just said that the only connection that you deemed usable was the teleprinter. Were you aware of the telegram link that existed between Pale and Banja Luka before the corridor was broken?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you had helicopters available to you in Banja Luka that you could use to travel outside of the ARK; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: No, not me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sajic, at paragraph 47 of your statement you described travelling to Knin by helicopter in mid-May. Does that remind you of the availability of helicopters at this time to travel outside of the ARK?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: There was a helicopter, but I didn't use it. I could not use it. I'm talking about myself. The helicopter, however, did fly to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you were in it; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. That's clear now. Moving on, Mr. Sajic. At paragraph 55 of your statement you said that some municipalities did not accept the decisions of the ARK Crisis Staff and they did not implement the conclusions that we adopted. And you then go on to give the example of Banja Luka resisting the ARK Crisis Staff. Now, when you testified previously in the Brdjanin case, you explained that you could, in fact, only speak about Banja Luka in this regard and you didn't know the extent to which other municipalities in the ARK accepted ARK Crisis Staff conclusions. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: At paragraph 68 of your statement you comment on adjudicated fact number 555 which regards restrictions on movement imposed on Muslims and Croats in the ARK, and your evidence is: "Restrictions on free movement were aimed at all citizens regardless of their nationality." Are you aware, Mr. Sajic, that on the 23rd of July, 1992, the Celinac War Presidency issued a decision on the status of the non-Serb population in Celinac and that decision, among other things, forbid non-Serbs from "moving around Celinac town between 1600 and 0600 hours," forbid them from "lingering in the street, catering facilities and other public places," and forbid them from travelling outside their settlements without permission from the authorities. That's P2638. Were you aware of that decision?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say that with the possible exception of Banja Luka, you don't really know in any detail what kinds of restrictions were placed on the movement of non-Serbs in ARK municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to come back to your 4th of May mobilisation order, and that order in addition to mobilising the TO, pursuant to General Subotic's order, also imposed a curfew and called for the disarming of paramilitary formations and individuals who illegally possessed weapons. Now, when you testified previously in the Brdjanin case, you confirmed that the disarmament provision and the curfew provision were based on your own assessment of the situation on the ground. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you also confirmed that these additions were consistent with General Subotic's order which instructs recipients to take all necessary measures based on the specific situation in their territories. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You also confirmed previously in your prior testimony that your mobilisation order of the 4th of May was mandatory. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when you testified previously you were read out the following passage from Miroslav Vjestica's speech at the 16th Assembly Session, which is P956, page 21, where he said: "As for Bosanski Novi, let me tell you that I was there yesterday. Bosanski Novi is sealed off. An ultimatum has been issued and a dead-line set for the Muslims to surrender their weapons. Some of them did, some did not. Yesterday there was shooting. What will happen today? I believe they will surrender. The same is going on in Sanski Most. I think the Muslims will soon be disarmed there too." And in your previous testimony you confirmed that Mr. Vjestica was talking about the results in Bosanski Novi of the 11th of May disarmament dead-line prescribed in your 4th of May order. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to P3928 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sajic, this is a Sanski Most SJB report of the 15th of June, 1992, on the process of disarming paramilitary formations in Sanski Most. And you can see in the first paragraph it states that the army, TO, and SJB have for some time been disarming paramilitary Muslim and Croatian formations in the Sanski Most area. And it says that peaceful disarming and surrendering of Muslims was carried out between 10th and 25th of May. During that period, the Muslim and Croatian population handed over only hunting weapons and other legally owned weapons, but illegally obtained military weapons were not surrendered. And then in the third paragraph it states that: "On the 25th of May ... the 'disarming' was followed by a military action (attack) against ... Mahala, where ... 2.000 civilians were captured but no significant amounts of weapons were found." Now, this document reflects the implementation of the disarmament aspect of your 4th of May order in Sanski Most, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 65 of your statement you talk about adjudicated fact number 538 which states that the ARK Crisis Staff disarmament demands were selectively enforced against non-Serbs. And you stated that you disagreed with this fact. You stated that: "Illegal weaponry was demanded from all regardless of ethnicity." Mr. Sajic, Mr. Vjestica's Assembly speech that I read to you a few moments ago and this Sanski Most SJB document refer exclusively to disarming Muslims and Croats. And it's true, is it not, that the ARK disarmament process was, at least for the most part, selectively enforced against non-Serbs, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I can give you my comment, but I stand behind my statement that illegal arming implies that an individual who doesn't belong to any unit owns a weapon. This applied to all ethnicities, even Serbs. Serbs also had illegal weapons. He took it from the army, refused to join his unit, and gave the weapon to his brother or cousin. Now, how it was applied in different territories, that's a different matter. But that demand was made of everyone. Now, how Vjestica put it in practice is something different. I cannot tell you about every municipality individually. The way it happened, it happened. But illegal possession of weapons is illegal possession of weapons. That demand was made of everyone, whether it was applied differently in Celinac than somewhere else, that's something different. And still, even after this drive, a lot of weapons remained hidden in houses as an illegal possession. But the requirement was made of everyone equally. I cannot give you the kind of answer you seem to expect like it was more on this side than another side.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, let me remind you of your prior testimony on this point. And this is from page 98 of 1D09818. And you were asked -- you were actually referred back to your previous OTP interview. You were asked: "I'd like to go back to your interview for a minute. During your interview with us, you talked honestly about who was disarmed. You were asked, talking about the order on mobilisation and disarmament: "'But the effect was this, wasn't it, that it was only the Muslims and Croats who were having their weapons removed from them.'" Your answer: "Mainly, you cannot say that it was a hundred per cent like that, but this statement can stand." And then you were asked: "And you were telling the truth, weren't you, sir?" And your answer was: "Yes." And that's correct, isn't it, Mr. Sajic? It may not be 100 per cent the case, but for the most part it was Muslims and Croats who were disarmed pursuant to your order in the ARK; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I have to repeat what I stated before on three different occasions. I'm not deviating from my earlier statements. It was required of everyone, regardless of ethnicity, to give up their illegally owned weapons. It's quite logical the way you draw conclusions, but I don't know which percentages you are thinking about. If there were more Serbs who were incorporated into units, it's quite logical that less weapons were taken away from Serbs. It's logical that more weapons were taken away from Muslims and Croats because they had received their weapons not from the army but from the HDZ and the SDA. I'm not retracting on my statement that more weapons were taken from Muslims and Croats, and that is a question to which you cannot answer yes or no. You have to give an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
