utterances.text: Mr. Sajic, you are emphasising that this was an order to disarm people from illegally possessed weapons, but it's true, is it not, that this disarmament order was also used to disarm Muslims and Croats of legally possessed weapons and you even knew of a case where a Muslim friend of yours had his legal weapon taken away. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I gave an example of this man called Islam. He did not get his weapon from a unit. He worked as a professional on the staff while I was working there. These are individual cases where legal weapons were taken away from somebody; I'm not denying that. But the order was to seize weapons in illegal possession, weapons that were not obtained from a unit or from people who refused to join the unit, whereas they had taken a gun. So if anybody abandons their unit, any unit, there were units which incorporated Muslims and Croats as well, there were even units that were -- that comprised entirely of Muslims so if he took the weapon and was not in the unit, that weapon was supposed to be taken away from the man.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sajic, I'd like to move to something else now. You said at paragraph 49 of your statement that Pale had deep reservations about the existence of the ARK and all its organs. And you said Pale's influence on Krajina was non-existent. You also explained at paragraph 22 that you were never an SDS member and, in fact, SDS members referred to you as a commie. The Trial Chamber has received a lot of evidence about the relationship between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Brdjanin, in particular evidence of meetings and phone calls between the two of them. Now, I take it you are not familiar with the details of their contacts such as when they spoke, what they spoke about, or the nature of their relationship; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I was not privy to all the conversations between Mr. Brdjanin and Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Were you privy to any conversations between Mr. Brdjanin and Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay, if we could go to 65 ter 05513, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sajic, this is a Banja Luka CSB dispatch of the 22nd of June, 1992. And it states that the ARK Crisis Staff has adopted the following decision which we give to you in full and then it repeats that ARK Crisis Staff decision from a 22nd June, 1992, meeting. And if you look at just under Roman numeral I of that decision, it says that: "All executive posts ... posts involving a likely flow of information, posts involving the protection of public property, that is, all posts of importance to the functioning of the economy may only be held by personnel of Serbian nationality." And on page 2 under Roman numeral II it states that: "The dead-line for implementing ... this decision ... is the 26th of June 1992 ..." And then after the decision the -- is repeated, the CSB chief, Mr. Zupljanin, gives instructions for its implementation in the C -- in the SJBs. Now, it's clear that compliance with this decision would require dismissing any Muslims or Croats holding the types of posts described in the decision; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: That's what the decision says; however, in practice it wasn't like that, it didn't have to be like that. In the public security centre there were Muslims and Croats, in the same centre where Zupljanin worked. In my own staff, there were Muslims and Croats on the staff. So I repeat, when you read all these decisions issued by the Crisis Staff, you can never be sure whether it was really done. If it was done to some extent, to what extent. In some cases none of it was ever put in practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, at paragraph 41 you said you did not believe that Brdjanin personally called for the dismissal of Muslims and Croats, but this document shows that through his position as ARK Crisis Staff president he did exactly that, called for the dismissal of Muslims and Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: From the documents it appears so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us be precise. Is this about dismissal or about replacement of people in executive posts?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: First of all, I'm not clear on that distinction. Secondly, I asked the witness that this would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now -- I would tender that document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6533, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sajic, a moment ago you said: "In my own staff there were Muslims and Croats on the staff." You're talking about the Banja Luka TO staff; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And then after paragraph 11 of your statement you discuss how the TO was reorganised into the 1 KK and the TO thereby ceased to exist; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And it's right that after the 1 KK was formed, Muslim and Croat officers were purged from the 1 KK; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: What do you mean "purged"? I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, maybe it will make it easier if I read from your prior testimony, and this is at page 151 of 1D09818. You were asked: "Now, you know, don't you, that in fact ultimately not right on this date," and the date in your reference is 9th of June, 1992, "but soon thereafter officers of Muslim and Croat nationality were purged from the 1 KK; correct?" And you answered: "I'm not trying to deny that, but I do not know the exact date when these officers were purged or who exactly was purged. I don't know the date, whether it was on the same day or not. I can see this order by Mladic and it looks quite clear to me." And then you're asked: "I'm not asking you for the day. I just wanted your confirmation that that, in fact, occurred, that these men of Muslim and Croat nationality were, in fact, purged from the 1 KK ranks; correct? Don't worry about the exact day." And your answer was: "Yes." And that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: It's true that I made that statement, but you cannot read that statement as saying that the corps was purged of all the Muslims and Croats. But when I was giving my statement, I said that many of them -- in fact, several of them started and ended the war being members of the 1st Krajina Corps. When I talked about this subject, I meant primarily active-duty officers. There was, for instance, one colonel, I can't remember the name now -- I meant active-duty officers. The reserve force was composed of people who were born there, natives of these areas, who stayed to defend their homes, members who -- of the former Territorial Defence which was renamed a brigade and they remained as members of the brigade. I cannot say that they didn't stay there until the end of the war. We cannot generalise like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I would like to tender what I just read out, if Your Honours would like to see it, it's page 151 and 152.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, shall we take a look?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Of 65 ter 1D09818. It's the bottom of page 151 and the top of 152.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see that document that this passage in the transcript refers to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Can we take a look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be shown in Serbian? This is in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the 9th of June document that's being discussed here is in evidence at P5429. If Dr. Karadzic wants to raise it in re-direct, he's free to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive these two pages.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6534, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sajic, a few moments ago when I showed you the CSB dispatch repeating the ARK Crisis Staff decision, stating that only Serbs could hold certain types of posts you said: "So I repeat, when you read all these decisions issued by the Crisis Staff, you can never be sure whether it was really done." And then you said: "In some cases, none of it was ever put into practice." Back in 2001 when you were interviewed by the Prosecution, you were asked whether in 1992 Muslims and Croats were dismissed in Banja Luka. You said: "Mainly, yes, I agree to a large extent." And that's true, isn't it, Mr. Sajic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You also --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, under this number I get something else, P05429, it must be a different number.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'll get the reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sajic, you also told the OTP in 2001 that most properties that were destroyed in 1991 and 1992 in Banja Luka belonged to Muslims and Croats, and that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sajic, at paragraph 34 of your statement you said you attended five or six ARK Crisis Staff meetings and that General Talic only attended the first Crisis Staff meeting that you attended. But in addition to General Talic's presence, General Vujinovic, the assistant commander of the 1 KK for civilian affairs, attended several ARK Crisis Staff meetings on behalf of the corps. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Say, that's General -- in fact, Colonel Vujinovic, who was in charge of civilian affairs. That's literally nothing to the corps commander. He just gave his formal ascent. He was not a general. He was supposed to be promoted into general, but the active-duty officers did not agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Sajic, it's your evidence that the assistant commander for civilian affairs is nothing to the corps commander? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: A person of very little import in the corps command. There were many more important people in the command of the corps, and he never replaces the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But -- Colonel Vujinovic did attend several ARK Crisis Staff meetings on behalf of the corps and he reported on those meetings to his command. That's what you said before and that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Well, he should have reported. He was supposed to report. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It may be okay, but I wonder whether he -- in line 8: He never replaced the commander. Should it be he never deputised the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We understood it in that meaning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sajic, just so we're clear, Colonel Vujinovic did attend several ARK Crisis Staff meetings on behalf of the corps, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, he's from the corps. He didn't have any kind of authority. He just attended. Please understand me. It is one thing to attend on behalf of the commander and to make decisions on behalf of the commander and it's a different thing just to be present. He could not replace the corps commander. He did not have the authority to deputise for him. It is only Kilecevic [phoen] who had that kind of authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do Your Honours wish to break now? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 1.20. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.34 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sajic, at paragraph 50 of your statement you describe regular Monday meetings of the Crisis Staff attended by municipal -- municipality presidents where reports were supposed to be provided to Dr. Karadzic. And then at paragraphs 56 and 58 you describe one of those meetings in more detail, it's a meeting attended by representatives from Prijedor and there was a discussion of camps. Now, was it Mr. Stakic, Mr. Drljaca, and Mr. Kuruzovic who attended that particular meeting as the Prijedor representatives?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you're asking. They did not submit their report to Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, I was just reading from your statement. My question is: At the ARK Crisis Staff meeting where there was a discussion of camps and, in fact, an argument between the Prijedor representatives and Mr. Radic, a meeting you describe, was it Mr. Stakic, Mr. Drljaca, and Mr. Kuruzovic who attended from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I gave that -- well, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And Mr. Brdjanin chaired that particular meeting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 58 of your statement you said that the Prijedor representative reported that there was a shortage of food and clothing in these camps and they didn't have sufficient accommodation for these people. And you characterise this as "the usual problems facing collection centres at the time when there was a high concentration of people in a small space." I take it from this that it was clear to you and everyone else at this meeting that large numbers of non-Serbs were being held in collection centres in the ARK; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know how many there were there. I was not at these collection centres, as I said in my statement; however, there was this problem that I refer to in paragraph 58. The problem was even more pronounced because the population and even the military to a large degree did not have enough food because there were other refugees coming from other areas. So the capacity of the Krajina was increased compared to the pre-war period.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sajic, you didn't really answer my question. At paragraph 58 you talked about "the usual problems facing collection centres at the time when there was a high concentration of people in a small space." Now, I put it to you that the only way that remark makes any sense is if it was clear to you and those at the meeting that there were large numbers of people being held in collection centres in the ARK at this time.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I can say yes, a large number is an abstract concept, it is not any particular figure, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And it was also clear that these people were non-Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I have one question about the SOS blockade in early April in Banja Luka that you talk about in your statement and it's just to have you confirm something you said before in 2001 to the OTP. And in 2001 you said -- you referred to a general -- sorry, a negative outpouring of feelings towards Muslims and Croats by the SOS. That's correct, isn't it, there was a negative outpouring of feelings towards Muslims and Croats by the SOS?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know that that's exactly what I had stated. Negative outpouring of feelings -- there were negative outpourings regarding things that happened in Sijekovac and many other places, negative outpouring because of the poor status of the army and so on and so forth. I don't remember saying that it was done because of the Muslims and Croats, that that was the only reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 25672, page 47 of the English and page 63 in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is a page from your -- the transcript of your tape recorded interview with the Prosecution in 2001, and near the top in the English about a third of the way down in the B/C/S you were asked: "You did not approve of the SOS and its activities; correct?" And you answer: "In my opinion, they were needless just like in September 1993." And you're asked: "Now surely you remember that one of the demands made by the SOS to the senior SDS leadership and military leadership in Banja Luka was that all Muslims and Croats in Banja Luka should be dismissed from their jobs?" And your answer was: "I don't know whether it was in that form presented, but one could say that there was this negative outpour of feelings towards that part of the population." And you're asked: "By the SOS?" And you say: "Yes." Now, in 2001 you told the Prosecution that the SOS had a negative view or negative feelings towards Muslims and Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I'm reading this here now. I don't know whether it was in such form, but - but again - one could say that the outpouring was -- I mean negative towards that -- anyone I guess. I don't understand this really. So negative outpouring, yes, since that's what happened in town, under the blockade, et cetera, but it wasn't only against the Muslims and Croats but against the Serbs too. I'll give you an example. The president of the Executive Board of Banja Luka, he was not allowed to enter his office. So the SOS did things that were not supposed to be done, not only against Muslims and Croats. And I already said that in my statement that that was not supposed to be done and that that did not enjoy any support on my part, and it also had to do with some Serbs, especially those criminals who would snatch earrings or chains or things like that. The SOS did not only go after Muslims and Croats. It was an unnecessary trouble for everyone in Banja Luka for three or four days.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6535, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sajic at --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have P956 now, page 20 in the English and page 17 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: While that's coming up, Mr. Sajic, at paragraph 54 you said that neither the republican leadership nor the strategic objectives presented at the RS Assembly ever had the goal of expelling Muslims or Croats from the territory of the RS. Now, you attended the 16th Assembly Session in Banja Luka when Dr. Karadzic presented those goals; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the document in front of you, this is transcript from that session that you attended, and this is Mr. Vjestica speaking shortly after Dr. Karadzic described those goals. And this is at the bottom of the English page and it is about a third of the way down for you, Mr. Sajic, in the B/C/S. And Mr. Vjestica says: " ... on the right bank of the Una river there are no more Muslims in the Serbian municipality of Bosanka Krupa. All the enclaves that were there, Rapusa, Veliki Vrbovik, Ostroznica, Babic, Muslim Jasenica and Zavir, we have evacuated them so that there will be none there for the duration of the war operations. Will they have a place to return to? I think it is unlikely after our President told us the happy news that the right bank of the Una is the border" --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: The problem is that the interpreter can't find the relevant paragraph and I suppose the witness too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's about 16 lines down from the top of the page where it begins, roughly a third of the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we show him the previous page to let him know this is what Mr. Vjestica said.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You see Mr. Vjestica's name about two-thirds of the way down, Mr. Sajic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go back to the previous page, i.e., the next page? So if you could read out again, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I will. And, as I said, this is, I think, 16 lines from the top in the B/C/S. Mr. Vjestica says: "On the right bank of the Una river there are no more Muslims in the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa. All the enclaves that were there, Rapusa, Veliki Vrbovik, Ostroznica, Babic, Muslim Jasenica and Zavir, we have evacuated them so that there will be none there for the duration of the war operations. Will they have a place to return to? I think it is unlikely after our President told us the happy news that the right bank of the Una is the border ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sajic, in your statement you said the strategic objectives did not have the goal of expelling Muslims and Croats from the RS. But Mr. Vjestica here at the 16th Session is saying essentially the opposite, isn't he, that the permanent removal of Muslims from territories defined by the strategic objectives is consistent with those objectives?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Am I supposed to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, it was a question. I'm asking you to confirm that what Mr. Vjestica said at this session, at which you were present, was that the permanent removal of Muslims from territories defined by the strategic objectives is consistent with those objectives?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I was present at the Assembly on the 12th of May up until I think Mladic spoke, and I have already stated that I did not attend the entire Assembly session. And finally, I wasn't even acquainted with these strategic objectives, but Vjestica often spoke about something but that doesn't mean that those were the objectives. He said, conditionally speaking, that he had cleansed whatever of Muslims and that it's a good thing that the president said that the border would be there. The president himself could not say where the border would be; it depended on military operations and ultimately on the Dayton Agreement. So I cannot accept that, that the leadership reached such agreement that there would be an ethnically cleansed Republika Srpska. That is my feeling, that is my conviction, throughout the war and ever since. That is my feeling and not only mine, also of many other people. So in the statement that I gave here, the republic leadership, et cetera, I believe did not have as a strategic objective any kind of cleansing. That would be my comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Firstly, Mr. Sajic, you talked about borders and you said: "The president himself could not say where the border would be ..." Have you forgotten at this session strategic objective 4, as announced by Dr. Karadzic, was the establishment of a border on the Una and Neretva rivers?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I repeat -- I mean, I didn't listen to all of it with regard to these strategic objectives, but an objective to have a border somewhere does not mean ethnic cleansing to my mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, you've confirmed that that was nevertheless what Mr. Vjestica was talking about. So if that was, as you say, a wrong interpretation by Mr. Vjestica about what the strategic objectives meant, then you would expect someone from the leadership, Dr. Karadzic or somebody else, to correct Mr. Vjestica so that the deputies aren't left with the misimpression that the strategic objectives are about ethnic cleansing, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I repeat, I don't know whether I listened to Vjestica at all on the 12th of May, 1992, I did not stay the entire Assembly session. That's why I cannot accept that I heard Vjestica, and even if I listened to all of this, it wouldn't mean that somebody accepted that. Vjestica is just Vjestica, just an individual. Even if it were an important office-holder, it cannot just -- well, that would be my answer. I cannot say a priori yes to something that I did not even listen to, and I repeat once again quite sincerely: The people did not have such objectives. The people did not think that there was any objective of cleansing the other peoples there. I assure you of that. I am from that area, the AR Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to P3656, please. This is the -- a report on the current political and security situation dated the 1st of June, 1992, by the 1 KK, and I'd like to direct your attention to the third paragraph of this document, approximately halfway through the paragraph it states: "A portion of the Muslim and Croatian population is moving out, and the Region of Bosnian Krajina has issued a decision to facilitate such departures, providing that the Serbs -- that Serbs from Central Bosnia and places with predominantly Muslim and Croatian populations were also allowed to move out. Those departing will not be allowed to return." Now, you just said that the people did not have the objective of ethnic cleansing and you say: "I assure you of that. I am from the area of the AR Krajina." Now, the decision of the ARK authorities described in this document, that Muslims and Croats who are moving out will not be allowed to return, reflects the implementation of the first strategic goal in the Krajina, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Could you please show me this entire document to the end? This is the first report on the current political and security situation. Could I just have a look at this document up to the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Certainly. It's three and a half pages, if you'd like to scan through it.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page now, Mr. Sajic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I haven't seen all of it -- well, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You're welcome to look at it, Mr. Sajic, but I can reassure you that nothing else in this document refers back to the passage I read out to you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: And finally the signature, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellent.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sajic, should I repeat the question for you? I will.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, the decision of the ARK authorities that Muslims and Croats who were moving out will not be allowed to return, that's described in this document, reflects the implementation of the first strategic goal in the Krajina, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I don't see that decision here. I see a document that the assistant commander for morale, Colonel Vukelic, is sending as a report, I don't know whether it was sent to Talic or the Main Staff, and he's presenting his view. I have to see a document where a body of the AR Krajina, that would be the Executive Council -- well, you keep saying "Crisis Staff," but I think that it's only for the Executive Council to say that, that that kind of decision was made -- I mean, there has to be a decision and this primarily referred to Serbs. If they were leaving, they were proclaimed to be traitors of their people and they were prohibited from returning ever. Now, Vukelic is commenting upon some decision as assistant commander for morale who just --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He is commenting upon this just as if I heard -- I mean, it's not meritorious, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sajic, can you -- the interpreters didn't catch what you said after: "... Vukelic is commenting on some decision as assistant commander for morale ..." Can you please complete that sentence?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: This is the opinion of Mr. Vukelic as the assistant commander for morale. In this document I don't see -- well, he is saying that the authorities of the Krajina made a decision. Which authorities is he referring to? What does he mean? Often in assessments, in reports, between the military and civilian authorities there would be a divergence; namely, both the civilian and military authorities were accusing each other. They were not opposing sides, but they kept accusing one another and they kept making poor assessment of each other so military personnel criticised civilian authorities and then the civilian authorities criticised military personnel. This happened at the level of the Krajina, and I personally think that this happened even further up at higher levels. That is why I cannot accept this statement. To that I would like to add the following: I was against any kind of moving out until the corridor was established. As far as I can see, this is the 1st of July, is it? What is the date here? I do not see the date. Could I have the first page once again, please. The 1st of June, yes. And he is submitting information to his commander, and the commander lives in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sajic, I'd like to remind you of what you said previously when you were shown this document, and that's at 65 ter 1D09818 at page 167.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's coming up on your screen and it's in English only so I will read it to you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And there was a rather lengthy discussion about this document and ultimately the Judge asked you: "The question is doesn't it make sense that the decision in Bosnian Krajina that Muslims and Croats who leave are not going to be allowed to return because strategic goal number 1 is not to be in the same state as Muslims and Croats. This is the question. "In other words, you are being asked to confirm that the decision of the ARK Crisis Staff that those who leave will not be allowed to return fits in the first strategic point mentioned or outlined by Krajisnik according to that report." And I just mention that there is a mistaken reference to Dr. Karadzic at the 16th Session. And you answered: "To leave room for those who will be coming from elsewhere, the Serbs coming from other parts. In that sense, yes." And then you're asked: "Right. In the sense that Bosnian Muslims and Croats who leave will not be allowed to return, period, and you're saying the rationale behind that is to allow Serbs to move in; right?" And you answer: "It is linked up in the text. In the statements, it is all linked up. Yes."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where is Karadzic mentioned here, please, can you tell me? The Prosecutor said that those were my words or that those words are in relation to what I said. Line 24, line 25, she says that it has to do with my own words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What Ms. Gustafson said is "Krajisnik" is mistakenly referred to by -- who?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: They were referring back to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- announcement of the strategic goals at the 16th Session, and by counsel and then by the Judge it was mistakenly attributed to Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it should read "outlined by Karadzic," that's what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes. And it refers back to the 16th Session, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sajic, that's what you said before when you were shown this document, that the decision that Muslims and Croats who move out will not be allowed to return was consistent with the strategic objectives and the rationale was to allow Serbs to move in; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I don't quite get it. One thing is what I said during the Brdjanin case and the other thing is what you're asking me now. I don't even know whether I ever saw this ARK document on a ban on return, that decision was never shown me. That's one thing. Second of all, I'm not denying what I said as a witness against Brdjo. However, the question is now put in a different context. If you were to ask me whether the moving out of Muslims was carried out or -- in an organised manner, I would say no. If you ask me the same question in a different way, I would say yes. This is a very vague question, so I can't say either yes or no. I would have to provide a lengthy explanation to tell you which part merits a yes answer and which part merits a no answer. You have to be more precise, and only then will I be able to give you a good-quality answer; otherwise, I can't do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sajic, you just -- you took issue with my question, claiming that I was referring to something different and that you'd never been shown this 1 KK document before. And if we could just go back to page 157 of this transcript where this line of questioning includes reference, specific reference, to this document. Two-thirds of the way down --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Objection. It is not correct that the witness said that this document was never shown to him. He said that the decision that Vukelic is talking about was never shown to him. This is not the way to interrogate and examine a witness. Einstein himself would be confused by this manner of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'll ask it this way then.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sajic, you don't deny that what I just read you from the transcript was a question based on the same 1 KK document that I just showed you, right, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I looked at that document properly. I'm now reading the document in detail and I'm telling you that I did not peruse it in detail at the time. This document doesn't mean anything in the sense of the decision on moving out. This is just Mr. Vukelic's opinion. I don't want to be harsh on him, but he was often -- let me not go there. Second of all, he was not in a positions where he would have been able to provide such qualifications, and I underline once again that the animosities often existed between the active military personnel, i.e., military authorities, and civilians. This is a tendentious type of writing in my view. On the 1st of June, on the 1st of June, that is, what was still valid, and I claim that, that we were staying in the territory of Krajina. And now on to Banja Luka, that we were staying together, Croats, Muslims, and Serbs, and that we would share the common lot because the corridor was closed. You, I'm sure, are aware of that case of the 12 babies who died. So this was on the 1st of June. I personally was against the moving out of the Muslims and Croats. Irrespective of how this was conveyed to me, I couldn't accept that. I would not have been able to accept that. I was not even aware of the date. I want us to discuss this document well and sincerely. This is not a credible document for the Trial Chamber. He writes about the status of morale --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is speaking too fast. It's impossible to interpret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Interpreters -- Mr. -- just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please understand me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters were not able to follow you because you spoke too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I repeat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could repeat from where you said he wrote about the status of morale.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vukelic wrote about morale, about morale in the army, and when describing the state of morale in the army when he spoke about high level of morale, he was explaining what was going on in various theatres of war which should have been done by operative organs. I'm not talking about his relationship with Commander Talic. However, Mr. Vukelic, and I underline, was not authorised to give his assessments. And this is just an assessment, this is not a decision, this is not evidence, this is just his opinion about the moving out of Muslims and Croats. And I would like to try and convince you that at that time in the months of May and June could have used some channels to move out of Krajina. But the general position across Krajina was that we should share the common lot and the breakthrough of the corridor happened on the 28th of June. That's when the territory of the -- the territory of the ARK with Serbia and the territory of Serbia were linked.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you've now had ample opportunity to comment on this document and you're now moving away from my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to tender these two pages of the transcript, page 167 and 168.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it. Have you admitted this part of transcript? I don't --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, but if it could be added to P6534 which is another passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 65 -- oh, yes, these pages will be added to that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sajic, in paragraph 67 [sic] of your statement, you discuss an ARK delegation visit to Omarska and Mr. Radic's negative impressions of what he saw, that he subsequently conveyed to you. Just to be clear, Mr. Radic told you that as they approached Omarska camp the detainees were forced to raise three fingers in the air and sing songs about Greater Serbia and this is what made Radic very uncomfortable; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: They were not forced to do that. They just did it and this is the difference. I can confirm what I said, but I cannot say that somebody approached them and told them to raise their hands. As they approached them, they would raise three fingers and sing songs about Serbia. They did it spontaneously. I don't know whether somebody from the camp threw stones at them and ordered them to lift their three fingers. They were not forced. Nobody forced them. If somebody used that term, they did it of their own will. But, yes, they did raise three fingers and they did sing songs about Serbia and, yes, I did hear that from Radic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 14, the paragraph should be "57" and not "67," as it is currently recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sajic, do you honestly believe that a group of Muslim and Croat detainees would spontaneously begin singing songs about Greater Serbia and raise three fingers in the air and you honestly believe that that would make Mr. Radic uncomfortable? It's quite obvious from the context that this was something that detainees were required to do; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: He didn't tell me anything about people being forced to do that. He said as they approached the camp that they raised three fingers in the air and sang, and he didn't tell me that somebody asked them to do that. He was a war orphan, as I already explained, and that's what made the situation difficult for him. He never told me that somebody whipped them and forced them to lift those three fingers. He never said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And just to be clear --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: The fact is that they did raise three fingers and the fact is that they did sing those songs.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the significance of the raising of the three fingers is that that's a traditional Serb salute, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm not following you. You said -- you said they were not forced to do so; correct? You said: "They were not forced. Nobody forced them." Is it your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said that Radic told me they had raised three fingers and sang songs and that I never said that he had told me that those people were coerced into doing that. In other words, he never told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're talking about words being added to what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I can understand, but today's transcript just a minute ago it is noted as this. You said: "They were not forced. Nobody forced them." If -- do you still stand by that evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I did not say that. I said that I don't know whether they were coerced. I didn't say that they did it of their own will or that they didn't do it of their own will. I can repeat. I wasn't there. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sajic, at paragraph 42 of your statement you discuss Mr. Brdjanin's statements to the media about Muslims and Croats. Now, this paragraph doesn't 100 per cent reflect what you said before so I'd just like to confirm a few things that you said previously about this. First, you learned from other Serbs in Banja Luka that Mr. Brdjanin had said in the media that only a thousand Muslims would be allowed to stay in Banja Luka and they would be elderly people who'd be put to work cleaning the streets. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: You think that I said that to -- during the Brdjanin case or that I said that to the investigator? What do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm just asking you if it's true, Mr. Sajic, that you heard from other Serbs that Mr. Brdjanin said in the media that only a thousand Muslims would be allowed to stay in Banja Luka and those would be elderly people who'd be put to work cleaning the streets?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: And where did I state that?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If you deny it, we can go to your prior testimony. Do you deny that this is true?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Where? In what part? Well, I can't remember. The only truth that I know is that Brdjanin often spoke things that were not correct, that his mouth ran away with him. I could have heard from other people. I'm not saying that I didn't. I'm not denying that, but in what context, I don't know, but, very well, we can go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think it's a simple question but let's go to 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One sentence is completely missing. The witness said: I never heard him say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we go to 65 ter 1D09818, page 102 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this please be checked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't matter. We are coming to this transcript. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: About two-thirds of the way down you were asked: "I want to ask you a little bit about some of the things Mr. Brdjanin said when he was president of the ARK Crisis Staff, and perhaps just before he became president as well. One of the things you were asked about in this interview that you remembered was hearing from other Serbs that Mr. Brdjanin had said in the media - doesn't say whether it's TV or radio - that only a thousand Muslims will be allowed to stay in Banja Luka and that those thousand Muslims will be comprised," so the next page, "of elderly people who will be put to cleaning the streets. "Now, do you remember hearing about that from Serbs in Banja Luka, that they had heard Mr. Brdjanin say that in the media, as you state in the interview? "A. Yes." Now, that's what you said when you testified before and that's the truth; right, Mr. Sajic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I don't have that translation before me of that part of my testimony. Everything I have is in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: There is no B/C/S. That's why I read it to you verbatim. That's what you said when you testified before and that's the truth; right, Mr. Sajic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, let me answer, I did not hear any such nonsense from Brdjanin, any -- no such nonsense did I hear from him. I could have heard from other people and say yes to that question. So let my answer to your question be yes. But do you understand me, I personally never heard any such nonsense from him and he really did say a lot of things.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page of the transcript in the middle of the page you're also asked: "You can confirm to me, can't you, that Mr. Brdjanin made these types of speeches in the media? "A. Yes." So you also confirmed in your prior testimony that the more general point that Mr. Brdjanin made these types of derogatory speeches in the media; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I can confirm that Brdjo did deliver such speeches in the media. I said that when I was here, I don't know when. And now about the thousand Muslims who would be allowed to stay to clean the streets, and you have just read it out again, I did not hear that stupid statement, but I may have heard it from other people. If I had heard it, that figure would have stuck. He did say a lot of stupid things. I'm being serious. Him and Vukic said a lot of things, and I said that on day one when I provided my statement. So I may have heard it from other people, not from Brdjanin, but he did used to say a lot of stupid things; I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you have confirmed that these kinds of speeches about Muslims and Croats would put fear into the minds of Muslims and Croats who heard them and that they did, in fact, frighten the Muslim and Croat population; that's right too, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: The first sign of instance -- insecurity among Muslims and Croats in Banja Luka was when an influx of refugees came from Croatia, those Serbs who came from Sijekovac and all those developments after the events of April and May including Dobrovoljacka Street and Cazinska [phoen] Street. And after that they obviously started feeling insecure and that's what they started saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sajic, you didn't answer --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Line 6, witness said: From Sijekovac where the Serbs have been slaughtered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sajic, you didn't answer my question. I'll just read out what you said in your prior testimony which is on this same very page and the lawyer is referring back to your OTP interview. He's quoting from it. And the question is: "And you were then asked: 'These sorts of words would put fear into the minds of Muslims or Croat who were listening to them, wouldn't they?' And your answer was: 'Of course.'" And then in your testimony you said: "Yes." And then you were asked: "Then you were asked whether the point of this, of these speeches, was to frighten Muslims and Croats into leaving." And you said: "Well, I don't know whether that was the idea, but certainly they were afraid." So again you're confirming that these speeches frightened the Bosniak and Croat populations. And your answer in your testimony you said yes. That's true and that's what you said; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only three or four questions. I would like to call up 5469 which is Mladic's reply to Colonel Rankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please tell us, Lieutenant-Colonel, what is the meaning of the words: Send people to the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to deal with their status in service. When is somebody put on stand-by; i.e., when are they referred to the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: On the screen I don't have anything. I don't have a translation or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me read this for you. It says Muslim and Croat officers - and this is a reply to a telegram - should immediately be sent on vacation. Start the procedure for them to be referred to the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in order to deal with their status and service. What is this? Is this their demotion or what?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: In practical terms this implies the following: All the officers in the Army of Republika Srpska, the current Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the army of the so-called Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia came from the JNA. The status of the JNA was kept by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia composed of Serbia and Montenegro. So those officers had to be returned. For example, somebody is in their work-place and then they are reassigned back to their old work-place. This was not people being dismissed. This was sending them to Belgrade where they would be given a new job. This is the proper interpretation of the order sent to the 1st Krajina Corps. I believe that there was the 33rd Regiment which actually kept those officers on their ledger and paid them. Those Croatian and Muslim officers received salaries, but they were never active members of that unit. I don't know if you're happy with my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant-Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: So this is not about people being chased out from that unit. This is about sending them on vacation and on reassigning them. This was a common principle in the former JNA. For example, you serve in one region and then you are sent to serve in another region, you're transferred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can the witness please be shown P6533.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Something has remained unexplained about this document. It has been suggested that people were dismissed, that they were demoted. Let's look at page 2 in this document. Below number III I'll read out to you how Zupljanin interprets this. He says: "However, employees may not be dismissed or removed from posts without the knowledge of the CSB as has happened in some stations. Instead, appropriate solutions must be found for their reassignment to duties and work which are not in contravention of item I of the decision ..." Lieutenant-Colonel, does a change in a senior post mean dismissal from work according to this document?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: This is staffing policy. I think it was even called at that time the levelling of cadres. For instance, if a new party comes into power in a multi-party state, this ruling party assigns its own people to senior posts. It doesn't mean that the person who occupied it before lost their job. If people are dismissed unlawfully they can always sue and they will win the case, but this is not about dismissal. This is about transferring people to some other job for which they are qualified and have adequate education. And Zupljanin is perfectly right here, and indeed things were not done as Brdjanin would have wanted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What -- have you exhausted your questions about this, Mr. Karadzic? Otherwise, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, concerning the document I want to know if replacing somebody from a senior post means simultaneously dismissal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 54, line 16, you were asked about document P2638 concerning the restrictions of the rights of some Muslims in Celinac. Did you understand that this was a reference to non-Serb population or Muslims in general as opposed to certain individuals? How did you understand it?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The witness said he didn't know anything about the decision at all, so asking him to clarify details about it doesn't make any sense to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Could the parties please read the document about some people who were not detained, only their movement was restricted allegedly for their safety --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now these are just submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can raise it in your closing argument. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 65 it was put to you that the property of most Muslims and Croats, or rather, mostly Muslim and Croat property was destroyed or devastated. Tell me, what was the attitude of the authorities in Banja Luka and Krajina to the destruction of property? Was -- were the authorities involved and how did they treat this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I can only repeat my comment from before concerning the destruction of property. In that wretched war, what happened was that there were criminals of both Muslim, Serb, and Croat ethnicity and they got along very well between themselves. They would come, loot, get away. They got along well. I gave you an example of the Latas municipality where a Croat sold abandoned Croat houses to some Serb; however, the municipal authorities of Krajina were all against the destruction of property. And of course the most vulnerable population -- in fact, the most vulnerable property was the property of Muslims and Croats because people had weapons. There was always somebody who had been in a unit that had been issued a weapon and they would use it for that purpose, but the authorities were against any destruction of property.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 57 it was suggested that based on the order that had been forwarded to you, a number of civilians had been captured in Sanski Most -- in fact, the order was forwarded my you. Did your order imply any arrests of civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: No, never. My order and my decision governed the seizure of illegally owned weapons and the disarming of paramilitary units belonging to any ethnic community, illegal weapons not arrest of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the last question. Pages 51 and 52 you mentioned intelligence communications centre in municipalities. Which means of communication did these centres have and since what time have they been in existence in municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia there were republic and municipal centres of warning and information. That's what they were called. They were formed at the level of municipalities and there was duty service and there -- at the level of regions, Zenica, Sarajevo, Tuzla, Mostar, and some others, and I have to mention that my region, the ARK, basically coincides with this and at the level of Belgrade. These were centres for warning and alerting and information. They were used in peace time and in war time, as they had been during our civil war. They were used to warn and alert people to natural disasters and all sorts of accidents and emergencies. They were established and operated in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the 1990s. If somebody had pulled out this centre from Sarajevo to Pale, they could have managed the territory of Banja Luka, et cetera. I think I sent my decision through that centre. I'm not sure now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber where were the main hubs of that type of communication, in which places and under whose control?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: The main hubs were in Banja Luka, Tuzla, Zenica, Sarajevo, and Mostar. They were under the control of the Ministry of Defence, that is to say the secretariat for National Defence, the so-called military departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And out of those six how many were under Serb control when the war began?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Only Banja Luka. Banja Luka is the regional centre, but every municipality had its own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To what extent were these centres dependent on electricity and other amenities?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: They still depend on their power supply and the power supply in the time we're discussing was very fractious. There were power cuts and then power generators using electricity would be used, but it was a great problem to maintain this centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Lieutenant-Colonel, Mr. Sajic. Thank you for coming. Thank you for the effort you made to testify.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then that concludes your evidence, Mr. Sajic, in this case. On behalf of the Chamber I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is the next witness ready, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before we begin with the next witness, I just wanted to raise something with Your Honours that Mr. Tieger has discussed with Mr. Robinson. And it is, Your Honours, that I'll be asking and time may be on my side, but I'll be asking for the cross-examination of this witness to go over until tomorrow morning. Given that he finished his testimony as a Prosecution witness in the Mladic case only yesterday morning, it's simply a situation where a few more hours will ensure that I'm effectively prepared to officially deal with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I think you have an issue with his previous interview?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Indeed. And in a submission that we filed last week, I foreshadowed that argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But to save time, the Chamber is of the view it will admit those pages referred to in the transcript. So I would like the parties to identify those page numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think Mr. Robinson will find those in the table of concordance that was attached to our submission, and I should just ask that he have someone double-check those page numbers given my difficulties with numbering sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic, please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we please make a short pause between questions and answers so that everything is properly recorded. Did you testify in the case against General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we call up transcript 1D9173.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, did you tell the truth there and do you still stand by everything you said?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I told the truth. I have nothing to change or add to that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to tender this transcript pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you have no objection to the admission of this transcript?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4124, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, shall we deal with the associated exhibits except for the -- his previous interview, which I discussed with the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. There are 15 associated exhibits, two of them a translation was not provided to the Chamber in a timely fashion and we apologise for that. We would ask that those two, if you could possibly consider them this evening and make a decision tomorrow, and those are 1D29064 and 24780B, and that B is for the two pages that were actually admitted in the Tolimir case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Further, with respect to 1D9454 referred to in transcript page 13030, the Chamber is of the view it is not relevant to this case. And 1D09458 referred to in transcript pages from 13140 to 13143, witness stated he never saw this document and he was not in the IBK at the time; and further, this document was not even tendered in Tolimir case. 1D5459, the Chamber is of the view that this does not form an indispensable and inseparable part. 65 ter 23604, likewise, this document does not form an indispensable and inseparable part; the witness does not sufficiently comment upon it. Also, the same applies to 23606 and I wonder whether the Prosecution has any other objection than the items that I referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, nothing additional.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll admit the remaining part of the associated exhibits tendered, and if the Defence is minded to tender those documents, it should lead live as well as showing the relevance of the document. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, excuse me, Mr. President. We won't be leading any of those live, but I would like to ask your permission and Dr. Karadzic's permission, we had an error and the state -- in the summary which was distributed is not actually the correct summary to be read with this witness. So if you don't mind, I would like to be able to read a short summary that we do have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have no difficulty with it. Please go ahead. The exhibit numbers of these associated exhibits will be assigned and distributed to the parties in due course by the Registry. Please continue, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, and we haven't distributed this text so I'm going to read slowly. Milenko Todorovic completed military high school in 1966, specialising in artillery. He received his first commissioned rank of second lieutenant in 1971. Beginning in November 1993, Milenko Todorovic was chief of the intelligence and security organ in the East Bosnia Corps of the VRS. He retired from the army with the rank of colonel. At the time of his retirement, he was chief of the security department of the 3rd Corps command of the VRS in Bijeljina. In mid-November 1993, Mr. Todorovic entered a temporary assignment as chief of intelligence and security of the command of the East Bosnia Corps headquartered in Bijeljina. After the fall of Srebrenica, Milenko Todorovic testified that a telegram came from the Main Staff that the East Bosnia Corps command should be engaged and should prepare accommodation at the Batkovici collection centre for an additional 1.000 to 1200 new detainees. Milenko Todorovic believes that the task of finding accommodation for the additional detainees came from General Tolimir. The expected 1.000 to 1200 prisoners never arrived at the camp and Milenko Todorovic was informed by General Tolimir that the idea was abandoned and to drop all further preparations for that task. Although he is not certain, Milenko Todorovic believes that at least 24 hours and perhaps two to three days passed between him receiving the task and his phone call with General Tolimir indicating the task had been abandoned. And that's the end of the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have further questions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellencies, just one. I would like to call up D2243.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, let me ask you about one circumstance. In your document dated 15 April 1992, which we can see before us, in paragraph 3, somewhere in the middle it says: "The largest number of enemy soldiers are soon exchanged ..." And so on and so forth. I'd like to ask you this: Can you tell the Trial Chamber which levels had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, just a second. Did you say this is his document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I believe so. The document was signed -- no, no, this is Popovic. But there is also another document by Todorovic. Can we see the following page. Within this document there is another document that was referred by Mr. Todorovic. Can we look at page 4 in Serbian. Go on, continue. It's 65 ter 25603. I have this document before me, 25603. This is the document that was forwarded by Mr. Todorovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this was one of your associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to ask Mr. Todorovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, at what levels could people be exchanged? How quickly could people be exchanged at the level of lower units and how could that be done at the level of the republican commission? What was the time that was needed to exchange people?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Let me answer in the following way: At the level of the East Bosnia Corps command there was a commission for the exchange of prisoners of war if they had enjoyed the status as combatants of the BiH. Exchanges took place at the moment when there were prisoners to be exchanged at the mutual proposal of the two parties. And the 2nd Corps of the BiH army had its headquarters in Tuzla and our East Bosnia Corps would talk. There was a routine in place, they would agree on a meeting at which they would discuss a possible exchange with the mediation of representatives of the International Red Cross which was compulsory. There was also a state commission for exchanges of prisoners who enjoyed different kinds of statuses. I wouldn't know much about that commission and I can't share many details with you, but I know that it existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the brigade level, at the level of lower units, did it ever happen that there were ad hoc exchanges on the same day when people were taken prisoner, if that was possible?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to come closer to the microphone --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you come closer to the microphone, Mr. Todorovic. Thank you. If you could repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not aware of any such example of exchange. I'm not saying that there were irresponsible people out there who may have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's look at line 4 where it says that people were soon exchanged. What does that mean in time-frame terms? What does it mean when it says "soon"?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: "Soon" or "quickly" means a couple of days to -- ten days to a fortnight at the longest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And those who may have committed crimes or were suspected of having committed crimes as combatants, how were they treated? Were they earmarked for quick exchanges, as it were?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: In Batkovici camp, as far as I know, we did not have anybody of whom we had learned that they had been involved in the commission of serious crimes. None of those people in Batkovici was ever processed before being exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. That would be all for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it, you concluded your evidence in the Mladic case as a Prosecution witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In that case, your previous testimony was tendered as a -- in lieu of your oral testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already said that I have nothing to add to my previous evidence. I wouldn't change anything because I said the truth and only the truth and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, did you lead the witness in the Mladic case?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, I did not, but his previous -- portions of his previous testimony and the interview were tendered as his 92 ter evidence in the Mladic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. So your testimony in chief in this case has been admitted in writing, i.e., through your testimony in the Tolimir case. And now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to start?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, it's not a cross-examination that's easily sort of compartmentalised or boxed up, Your Honour. And if I may, I would prefer to start, with your leave of course, tomorrow morning to conclude as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's fair enough. So, Mr. Todorovic, we'll adjourn for today and continue tomorrow morning. I'd like to advise you not to discuss with anybody else about your testimony. But before we adjourn, Mr. Robinson, I would like to hear the witness schedule for this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I was going to rise to indicate that tomorrow after we conclude the testimony of this witness, we have one further witness this week. However, he is not able to -- well, the 48 hours between his proofing, which occurred last night, and the beginning of his testimony wouldn't take place until Friday morning. So we're not in a position to ask that he be cross-examined until Friday morning. He's a detained witness and he was only able to arrive on the day before yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What witness, Dobrijevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: He's coming for next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was he not moved up?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: He was moved up from two weeks in advance until next week. We're taking steps to bring additional witnesses in the upcoming weeks because when we received the Prosecution's cross-examination estimates for December, we realised that we need more witnesses in those additional weeks. So we're taking steps to bring additional witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any observation to make, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, nothing in particular, Mr. President, except to note with respect to the witness whose cross-examination on Friday was discussed, it's not only a matter of a technical -- the technical timing of the 48 hours, but in this case the previous statement was expanded from 33 pages to 45 pages at what we consider the 11th hour plus creating a variety of problems which we may raise with the Court when -- on Friday. But -- so it's not simply a matter of the 48 hours but additional issues as well. So -- but -- with respect to the rest of the submission, no, I don't have anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The hearing is adjourned.
